study.title: Genesis 2 The rest of God, the garden, the commandment, and the creation of the woman
study.overview: Genesis 2 broadens the creation presented in the previous chapter, placing focus on humanity, the seventh day, the garden and the formation of the family. The chapter shows God as the Creator who concludes his work, separates a holy time for rest, places man in an environment of provision and responsibility, establishes a moral commandment and ultimately creates the woman for the fellowship of the couple. The final verse highlights the original innocence of the first couple, without shame before God and among themselves. Evangelical reading sees here foundations for worship, work, obedience, marriage, and human dignity.

outline.title: The seventh day: conclusion, rest and sanctification
outline.explanation: Creation is presented as a work completed by God. The seventh day is blessed and separated as holy, indicating a distinct time to celebrate the finished work of the Creator and remember that rest is also part of the divine order.

outline.title: The origin of man: dust and breath of life
outline.explanation: The text recapitus creation with an emphasis on human beings. Man is formed from the dust of the earth and receives the breath of God's life, at the same time showing humility of origin and dignity as a living creature dependent on the Lord.

outline.title: Eden, human vocation and commandment
outline.explanation: God plants the garden, puts man in it and gives him work and responsibility: cultivate and keep. It also gives generous freedom, but establishes a clear moral limit by forbidding the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, linking obedience to life.

outline.title: The original woman, marriage and innocence
outline.explanation: Adam's loneliness is declared not good, and God creates a help corresponding to him. The woman is formed of the man and brought to him, establishing the marriage union as an alliance of unity. The chapter ends with both naked and shameless, portraying purity and confidence before the fall.

study.context: The chapter presents itself as an unfolding of creation, with a special focus on humanity. The notes highlight that the seventh day functions as a model for the Sabbath of Israel and that the garden in Eden is described as a sacred space, separated from the surrounding world, similar to a sanctuary. They also observe that the text organizes human life around vocation, limit and communion, before any rupture of sin.
study.theology: Theologically, Genesis 2 states that God not only creates, but also orders, sanctifies and sustains. Divine rest does not suggest weariness, but conclusion and approval of the created work. Humanity is presented as unity of body and breath granted by God, which sustains human dignity and dependence on the Creator. The garden shows that work is not a curse itself; before the fall, it is mandate and responsible care. The limit given by God reveals that true freedom is always accompanied by obedience. Marriage appears as a divine institution, marked by complementarity, union and exclusivity. The absence of shame in the end expresses relational innocence and moral purity, contrasting with the shame that will arise after disobedience.

scholarViews.insight: The seventh day is the climax of the week of creation and becomes precedent for the weekly Sabbath of Israel, destined to celebrate the completed work of God and to be separated as holy.

Man is the center of this account because God, in forming it, also took care of his happiness and dignity, showing that the creation of the human being was not accidental, but pastoral and intentional.
The nakedness of the first couple indicates the absence of guilt and shame, because there was still no sin or disorderly use of the body; shame arises only with the entrance of evil.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to separate time to recognize the completed work of God and to rest in it?
How does the order to cultivate and keep the garden correct visions that treat work as mere punishment?
How does marriage, presented here, challenge relationship models based on utility, individualism or domain?
study.practice: This chapter invites the believer to honor God's rhythm between work and rest, treating holy time as an occasion for worship and gratitude. He also calls responsibility in daily labor, seen as a vocation received from the Lord. In the family and marital relationship, the text encourages mutual respect, purity, fidelity and recognition that human union is a gift from God. Moreover, the innocence of Adam and woman recalls that life before God should seek transparency, without masks, manipulative shame or exploitation of the other.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided offer interpretive readings on the Sabbath, the garden as a sanctuary and the relationship between man and woman; these readings are useful, but should not be treated as unique and undeniable definitions of the text. It is also not possible, based only on the notes, to identify with historical precision the location of Eden, nor to deepen the meaning of the original terms beyond what the commentators suggest.
